title: May all beings be happy
hookLine: put on your own mask first: is a wish for all beings like that?
tomorrow: what was said in the grove the night the Buddha died?

cards: Every flight safety talk says it: put on your own oxygen mask before helping others. It sounds selfish for half a second, and then it makes sense.
The Pali wish of loving-kindness, metta, has an old argument hiding inside it that sounds a lot like that announcement. The line is sabbe satta sukhita hontu: may all beings be happy.
And yesterday's question is the argument itself. Should you start with yourself? Two serious answers, each with a text behind it.

teach.b: First the words. Sabbe: all. Satta: beings.
Sukhita: happy. Hontu: may they be. Now the first view.
Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification says to begin metta with yourself.

Its reason is a verse from the suttas: search every direction with your mind and you'll find no one dearer to you than yourself; in the same way, everyone holds themselves dear; so whoever loves himself should harm no one else.
The best case for this view: your own wish to be happy is the one you know from the inside. Feel it clearly, and you know everyone else's.
Starting with yourself isn't the goal; it's the doorway to seeing that all of us are alike in this. Now the second view.
The Metta Sutta itself doesn't start with you. It goes straight out wide: beings weak or strong, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born. May all be happy.

And then the picture of a mother guarding her only child with her life, and a heart like that, boundless, toward every being. The best case for this view: nobody gets left out, not even the ones you'd forget.

how: In Theravada temples, sabbe satta sukhita hontu often closes a chanting session or a sitting, and the Metta Sutta is among the verses monks chant for blessing.

games.q: what does “may all beings be happy” mean?
o: a prayer asking the gods to grant luck
a wish of loving-kindness for every being
a blessing that only monks may give out

games.q: the wish, word by word — tap the pairs.

s: the Metta Sutta starts its wish with yourself
it goes straight out to all beings; Buddhaghosa's handbook is the one that starts with yourself.
Buddhaghosa's reason comes from a verse in the suttas
no one is dearer to you than yourself, and everyone holds themselves dear, so harm no one.
starting with yourself means the wish stays with you
in the handbook, yourself is the doorway; the wish then goes out to others.

games.q: you've always started metta with yourself. a friend starts wide, with all beings, as the sutta does. what's the strongest case for her way?
o: nobody gets left out, not even the beings you'd forget.
it's more humble, so it earns more merit than yours does.
it skips you, and wishing yourself well is always selfish.
games.why: the Metta Sutta goes out to beings seen and unseen, near and far, born and yet to be born. its strength is that no one is missed. the handbook's way has its own strength: you know the wish from the inside.

practice: Say the line slowly three times, sabbe satta sukhita hontu. The first time, let it include you. The second time, one person who comes to mind easily.
The third time, let it go out as wide as it will go, then sit in whatever is left.

wordCard.voice: May all beings be happy. Sabbe satta sukhita hontu: the wish of metta, whichever door you enter by. Word twelve of a little Pali.

orig.note: sabbe satta sukhita hontu in Devanagari letters: may all beings be happy.

carryVoice: The line to hold: sabbe satta sukhita hontu, may all beings be happy, you included. Twelve days in.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.8 / Khuddakapatha 9, Karaniya Metta Sutta (all beings, weak or strong ... seen or unseen, near or far, born or to be born; the mother and her only child; a boundless heart)
Visuddhimagga IX (metta begun toward oneself), citing the verse of Samyutta Nikaya 3.8 / Udana 5.1 (no one dearer than oneself; so others hold themselves dear)
